[When no existing skill fits](#when-no-existing-skill-fits) - [What is included](#what-is-included) - [Go deeper](#go-deeper) - [Responsible use](#responsible-use) - [License](#license) ## What is HunterStick? HunterStick is a model-independent workspace for AI-assisted bug bounty hunting and web penetration testing. It gives a capable terminal agent two things ordinary AI chats lose: **focused fieldcraft for the current objective** and a **durable target brain** that survives context compaction, new sessions, long gaps, and model changes. You choose the target and the task. The model loads only the relevant skill and target context, works that objective to its exit criteria, stores the evidence and context delta, and stops. The next session — or a different model — continues from the same verified state instead of starting again from chat history. HunterStick is not an autonomous scanner and it does not decide the next objective for you. It is a context, fieldcraft, and execution harness for a hunter working with an AI collaborator. > **Supervised beta.** Review active commands before they run and the files they change. Use > HunterStick only on systems you are authorized to test; see [Responsible use](#responsible-use). ## Why AI bug hunting loses the thread Recon tools already enumerate, probe, and scan better than a language model. The model's advantage is connecting evidence, adapting a test, and reasoning across the target. That advantage disappears when its working context becomes unreliable. - **A context window is not target memory.** It compacts, closes, and eventually loses exact details. “We tested IDOR” may survive while the principal, endpoint, variant, and response do not. - **A new session or model starts cold.** Useful decisions remain trapped in yesterday's transcript unless someone reconstructs them by hand. - **Raw output crowds out reasoning.** Forty thousand lines of recon consume context without telling the model which forty assets deserve attention. - **General prompts create general behavior.** A broad “hunt this target” prompt mixes recon, analysis, testing, and reporting without a clear input contract or stopping point. - **Cross-context connections are missed.** An endpoint found in JavaScript on day one may matter only after the account model is understood on day five. A weak primitive may become exploitable after a later trust relationship is discovered. - **Coverage becomes a story rather than a fact.** Without structured records, sampled, failed, and one-principal tests are easily remembered as complete testing. ### What HunterStick changes | AI failure | HunterStick mechanism | Result | |---|---|---| | Context expires or compacts | A persistent brain for each target | Exact state survives sessions and model switches | | Prompts are broad and unfocused | One skill file per objective | The model receives task-specific inputs, method, outputs, and exit criteria | | Raw output overwhelms the window | Remote raw artifacts plus compact local knowledge | Context is spent on decision-relevant signal | | Test history becomes vague | Runs, tested variants, coverage, and evidence records | Principals, limitations, and negative results remain explicit | | Facts remain isolated across time | Provenanced observations, properties, hypotheses, and linkage graphs | Later evidence can connect to earlier facts | | The agent continues on its own | One skill, persist, report, **STOP** | The hunter chooses every next objective | The result is not a “better prompt.” It is a repeatable environment in which the prompt, target context, evidence, and available tools are assembled for one bounded objective. ## How HunterStick works

The hunter selects one objective; the model loads focused context, completes it, records the result, and stops.

### 1. The hunter names the work The user selects a target and names one objective: enumerate subdomains, analyse a request, map an application, test IDOR on an endpoint, or run a named situation flow. HunterStick never inherits an “active target” from the last conversation and never silently chooses a new objective. ### 2. The runtime loads focused context The runtime first loads the global operating contract, then the named target's compact brain, and finally the one skill required for the task. Accounts, technology references, and other artifacts enter the context only when that skill needs them. The complete skill and playbook library is never loaded into every turn. When the task names one application—an exact host, host:port, URL, or a request containing a host—the runtime resolves its per-app brain and loads only that app's map, endpoints, and notes. It does not load every application in the engagement. A missing app map narrows the context rather than borrowing a sibling's data; multiple port-specific maps require the exact port. This selection is mechanical through [`app-context.py`](tools/app-context.py), so a new session or different model reconstructs the same application context. ### 3. Required inputs are verified Each skill declares the input roles it consumes. Preflight resolves those roles against the target brain. When a required input is missing, the model names it and the skill that can produce it. When the input exists, the requested skill starts; scope is context supplied by the hunter, not an extra model-controlled authorization gate. ### 4. The model loops inside the chosen objective The model reads tool help, checks the installed version, pilots unfamiliar flags on one input, and verifies the output shape before scaling. It adapts selectors, sources, and variants to what the target has actually shown. A failed command, misleading empty artifact, or incomplete variant goes around the loop again rather than becoming a confident zero. Work may run locally or through the VPS harness depending on the skill. Active HTTP commands use the recording and privacy harness; bulk reproducible output remains on the VPS. Local reasoning, request analysis, passive sources, browser work, and curated context do not require everything to be remote. ### 5. Evidence becomes target knowledge Raw output is not treated as memory. The model stores decision-relevant facts with provenance, records what ran and what it did not cover, updates affected attack-surface and coverage rows, and keeps pointers to the underlying evidence. Facts, hypotheses, and assumptions remain distinct. ### 6. The model hands control back The model reports the delta, evidence, and limitations, offers two or three conditional next actions, and stops. The user chooses the next skill. That decision starts a new bounded unit of work against a richer target brain. ## How the target brain works Each target has its own directory of readable Markdown and TSV files. There is no vector database and no hidden memory service. A human can inspect, diff, correct, and version the reasoning state. Inside that target brain, each deeply mapped application has a smaller brain under `applications//`: `map.md`, `endpoints.md`, and `notes.md`. Target-wide facts stay at the target level; one-app tasks load the matching application directory alongside them. This keeps shared context available without letting facts from `admin.acme.com` silently become facts about `shop.acme.com`. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Human decisions
Target activity
Collected evidence] B[Normalize and curate] subgraph C[Local target brain] C1[Target profile
Scope and standing decisions
Accounts when needed] C2[Observations
Applications and properties
Trust relationships] C3[Runs and hypotheses
Attack surface
Tested variants and coverage] C4[Findings
Evidence pointers
Confirmed, draft, rejected] end V[VPS raw store
Tool output, jobs, logs, loot] D[Brief, resume, and preflight] E[Model + one focused skill] F[New evidence
Coverage and context delta] G[Next session
or another model] A --> B --> C V -. evidence pointers .-> C C --> D --> E --> F --> B C --> G G --> D ``` ### What the brain remembers - **Target identity and decisions** — the target profile, the hunter's scope statement, target accounts, and standing decisions such as read-only areas or account-creation constraints. - **Observed knowledge** — applications, endpoints, technologies, behaviors, ownership signals, and trust relationships, each carrying its source and confidence. - **Work state** — which runs started or failed, what is worth investigating, open hypotheses, and exactly which `entrypoint × class × principal × variant` cells were tested. - **Human-readable progress** — `progress.md` shows scope-wide runs and a table grouped by each host/IP, including the skill, tool, exact redacted command and options, wordlist/input hashes, result, and evidence pointer. Set-based commands remain explicitly unresolved instead of being guessed onto every host. - **A browsable dashboard** — `tools/dashboard.py --all` renders a gitignored `dashboard.html`: a sidebar lists every target with status chips (open runs, resume points, staleness, probes, surface); clicking one loads open runs, the runs ledger, attack surface, testing state, the rendered `progress.md`, roots/DNS, and a brain-files age tab, hash-routed so refresh and back stay put. `accounts.md` is summarized to usable-principal counts, never rendered, so credentials stay out of every generated page. - **Evidence and dispositions** — request/response artifacts and the findings they support, including rejected cases so they are not rediscovered as new. ### How the brain connects low-severity primitives A fact that is weak on one host can become important when another application trusts that host. HunterStick preserves both sides of that relationship inside the same target brain: - Vulnerability primitives and candidates live in `findings/`, `hypotheses.md`, and `attack-surface.md`. - Observed host relationships live in `observations.tsv` as directed or symmetric edges such as `references`, `authenticates-via`, `shares-session`, `shares-secret`, or `shares-backend`. - [`kb.py chains`](tools/kb.py) walks multi-host trust paths. - [`target-graph.py --chains`](tools/target-graph.py) joins those paths to vulnerability primitives, identifies complete and partial chain patterns, and names the missing half worth investigating. The graph is derived from the readable brain every time; it is not a second database that can drift. Deriving a possible chain sends no traffic and does not turn a hypothesis into a finding. #### Example: open redirect on one host, OAuth on another Suppose `app.acme.com` has an open redirect and `auth.acme.com` runs an OAuth flow that accepts or references a callback on `app.acme.com`. Individually, the redirect may be low severity. Together, they suggest that an authorization response might reach the redirect and leak a code or token, raising the possible impact to account takeover. HunterStick handles that connection in stages: 1. The open-redirect artifact is stored against `app.acme.com`. 2. The OAuth surface is stored against `auth.acme.com`. 3. The observed directed trust edge from the OAuth host to the redirect host is recorded with provenance. 4. The derived graph recognizes the pairing. If one side is only a candidate, it reports a **PARTIAL** chain and names the missing proof. If the required primitives and edge exist, it reports a **READY chain hypothesis**. 5. The model presents validation as a next action and stops. It does not silently exchange an authorization code, cross an account boundary, or exercise account takeover. 6. If the hunter chooses validation, the vulnerability loop performs the smallest safe test with a controlled account and stores every request, response, primitive, connector, and impact claim in an [investigation chain](targets/_template/investigations/chain.template.md). “READY” means the brain has enough evidence to justify testing the composition; it does **not** mean the final impact is already proven. The chain becomes a finding only when stored artifacts support every required edge. Ask the model: ```text Show low-severity primitives and possible chains across acme hosts. ``` Then, if one is worth pursuing, name it as the next objective: ```text Validate the open-redirect to OAuth chain between app.acme.com and auth.acme.com using my controlled account. ``` Here “Host X” and “Host Y” are applications inside the same named engagement. Separate `targets//` brains are not merged automatically; relating two different programs or engagements requires an explicit user decision so one target's evidence is never written into another target's brain by accident. The load-bearing distinction is: > `attack-surface.md` records what appears worth investigating. `tested.md` records what was > actually probed. Subtracting the second from the first produces honest coverage. One request cannot mark a whole endpoint or vulnerability class complete, and a new principal or bypass family remains a new test. To see what has actually been done without reading the ledgers directly, open `targets//progress.md`. After VPS work, HunterStick pulls the small `logs/exec/*.json` command records and regenerates the view with `tools/progress.py targets/`. Secrets remain redacted; wordlists and other input files are named with their recorded hash so the run can be reproduced later. ### Local brain, remote bulk The local target directory holds what a model needs to decide and reason. The VPS holds what can be re-derived: bulk output, jobs, logs, and loot. HunterStick brings only the relevant extract into the brain and keeps an evidence pointer back to the raw artifact. If the VPS disappeared, the investigation should still be understandable. If the chat disappeared, the next runtime should be able to reconstruct the work from the target brain. That is how context compounds across tasks and models without turning the entire engagement into one enormous prompt. > **The model reasons, the tools verify, the files remember, and the hunter directs.** ## Looping and harness engineering HunterStick does not implement looping as an autonomous agent that keeps inventing work. It implements a **bounded reasoning loop inside one user-selected skill**. The loop may retry, reconfigure tools, test additional variants, or refute its own conclusion, but it cannot cross into a new objective on its own. When the selected skill reaches its exit criteria, the model persists the delta and stops. The method is split deliberately: - A **thin focused file** carries what is unique to the objective: required inputs, useful signals, target-specific traps, outputs, variants, and exit criteria. - A **shared method file** carries the reusable reasoning loop. Recon skills share [`skills/shared/_recon-method.md`](skills/shared/_recon-method.md); vulnerability classes share [`_master-vuln-hunting.md`](playbooks/vulns/_master-vuln-hunting.md). - The **target brain** supplies the current evidence and remembers every useful delta. - Small tools provide the mechanical harness around the model: resolve inputs, open the run, dispatch commands, capture artifacts, compute coverage, and expose failures. This keeps prompts focused without copying the same instructions into every skill. Improving the shared recon or hunting method improves every thin skill that uses it, while each skill remains readable and editable by a human. ### The shared harness Every recon and vulnerability-testing unit uses the same outer lifecycle: ```text resolve target → load one focused skill and its shared method → verify required inputs → open a run before traffic → loop inside the objective → validate and persist the evidence delta → report limitations and next options → STOP ``` The harness has five cooperating parts: 1. **Context harness.** The runtime loads the global rules, one target brain, one skill, and only the references that skill needs. The model works from current files rather than a growing chat transcript. 2. **Input harness.** `tools/preflight.py` resolves the skill's declared input roles. A missing required input is named together with the skill that produces it. Optional inputs narrow the run and become an explicit limitation. 3. **Execution harness.** A run row is opened before traffic. HTTP commands pass through `tools/vps-run.py`, which applies the privacy check and configured attribution before dispatching to the VPS. `tools/run.py` records the installed tool version, redacted command, input hashes, duration, exit status, stderr tail, and output artifact hash. Long runs use the wrapper's detached tmux mode, preserving the same direct scanner argv and validation contract. 4. **Evidence harness.** Success is judged from a fresh expected artifact, not from a banner or exit code alone. Known structured tools are parsed against their output contract; any extra fields a downstream parser needs can be declared per run. A stale file, malformed JSONL or a jsluice filename accidentally consumed as `-R` fails before it can become a false “zero.” Recon facts require provenance; vulnerability claims require a stored request and response. 5. **Exit harness.** The skill defines what completion means. The model records uncovered bounds or parked variants, updates the brain, reports the decision-relevant change, and returns control to the hunter. The harness does not generate one hard-coded command for every tool. Tool versions, flags, target behavior, and useful discriminators change. The model owns command choice; the harness makes known- bad invocations, fresh output and declared JSON/JSONL shape fail loudly, then records the execution. See [Adaptive tooling](playbooks/system/adaptive-tooling.md) and [Dynamic command construction](TOOLS.md#dynamic-command-construction). ### The recon loop Recon asks **what exists and what properties it has**. The selected recon skill defines the signal to collect, but the model must determine how the installed tools can produce that signal on this target. ```text declared inputs + bounded selector ↓ open run → inspect installed tool and --help ↓ calibrate target behavior → pilot on a small sample ↓ verify one record and declare the fields the next step consumes ┌─────┴──────────────────────────┐ │ wrong shape, noisy filter, │ signal is trustworthy │ timeout, or reachable source │ │ still untried ↓ └── adapt and repeat scale within the bound ↓ normalize facts and coverage ↓ reassess patterns → report → STOP ``` For example, a content-discovery skill asks for distinguishable paths, not “run this exact `ffuf` command.” If the application returns `200` for every nonexistent path, the model calibrates the soft-404 response, selects a useful discriminator such as length or body marker, configures the installed `ffuf` build, verifies several hits, and only then scales. If the result is still noisy, the loop adapts again rather than storing a plausible but false inventory. Wordlists follow the same rule: target routes, JavaScript, components, and technology choose the list; popularity does not. If the applicable public list is missing, the model may download it on the VPS, verify it, record its source, and let the execution record hash the exact file used. Recon is complete when the skill's objective is achieved for the declared selector and sources, with every bound and skipped dimension recorded. If the objective cannot be achieved, the run is closed as failed or partial and says exactly why; it is never converted into a clean zero. Discovering that another recon skill would be useful creates a next option—it does not silently start that skill. ### The vulnerability-testing loop Vulnerability testing asks **whether one observed surface violates a security property**. The shared hunting method supplies the reasoning scaffold, while one class file supplies where that class hides, its variants, minimal validation, false-positive traps, impact model, and novelty questions. ```text entrypoint + class + principals + recorded context ↓ orient from the brain and existing tested coverage ↓ understand the function and map source → transformation → sink ↓ write a specific hypothesis and true/false discriminator ↓ design the smallest non-destructive request ↓ execute and store the real request + response ↓ filter false positives and try to refute the result ┌─────────┴────────────────────┐ │ inconclusive or another │ resolved variant or │ planned variant remains │ minimum proof reached └── refine and repeat ↓ assess impact and novelty ↓ update tested/finding state ↓ report → STOP ``` The loop is measured in **variants, not time or payload count**. An authorization test records the entrypoint, class, principal relationship, and variant; a new tenant direction or parser format is not hidden under “already tested.” A blocked request is not automatically a negative, and a suggestive response is not automatically a finding. The model changes one variable at a time, checks the class-specific false-positive traps, retests reproducibility, and makes a separate attempt to disprove its own conclusion. If a primitive is confirmed, HunterStick captures the smallest safe proof and stops before broad cross-account access, privilege expansion, or multi-step exploitation. Those are new escalation decisions for the hunter. A vulnerability becomes a fact only when its request/response artifact, impact argument, tested variant, and novelty decision are stored in the target brain. ### Same architecture, different question | | Recon skill | Vulnerability skill | |---|---|---| | Question | What exists, and what does it reveal? | Does this surface violate one security property? | | Focused file supplies | Objective, inputs, signals, traps, outputs, exit criteria | Applicability, variants, minimal test, false positives, impact, novelty | | Unit of progress | Selector × source × artifact | Entrypoint × class × principal × variant | | Inner-loop trigger | Wrong tool, output shape, discriminator, rate, source, or timeout | Inconclusive oracle, untested variant, false-positive signal, or unresolved contradiction | | Evidence | Normalized output plus provenance pointer | Stored request and response plus reproducible interpretation | | Completion | Objective reached with bounds and limitations recorded | Planned variants resolved or parked, or minimum proof complete | Both sides update the same generated `progress.md` view: the scope-wide table summarizes bounded runs, while each exact host/IP gets its own table of skills, tools or vulnerability probes, redacted commands/options, input files and wordlist hashes, outcomes, and evidence pointers. ## Start here ### Requirements - Python 3.10+, Git, and a POSIX shell - An agentic runtime with shell and filesystem read/write access - a VPS for bulk recon - Optionally, BurpSuite MCP + Chrome MCP. ### 1. Install HunterStick ```bash git clone https://github.com/tarekmo0/bugbounty-workspace.git hunterstick cd hunterstick cp config.example.json config.json chmod 600 config.json $EDITOR config.json python3 tools/config.py check python3 tools/self-check.py python3 tools/graph.py --check python3 -m unittest discover -s tests ``` `config.json` stores machine configuration such as researcher attribution, VPS access, and passive source API keys. It is gitignored. Models use `tools/config.py check`, which reports missing values without exposing credentials; they must never read `config.json` directly. If you use a VPS, fill its connection fields and ask the model: ```text Set up or audit my configured HunterStick VPS using playbooks/system/vps-setup.md. ``` The setup file installs the external recon toolchain and data assets; it is separate from cloning this repository. Its verification section checks capability alternatives, wordlists, Nuclei templates, and that the recorder deployed to the VPS matches this checkout. ### 2. Choose a runtime and model Claude, GPT, Kimi, and DeepSeek are model families. Claude Code, Codex CLI, Kimi Code CLI, and OpenCode are runtimes that give a model access to HunterStick's files and tools. Use whichever combination you prefer; the target brain remains the same. #### Claude — Claude Code Install [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/getting-started), then open the repository: ```bash cd hunterstick claude ``` `CLAUDE.md` points Claude Code to the canonical `AGENTS.md`, and `.claude/skills/` exposes the focused skills for on-demand loading. #### GPT — Codex CLI Install [Codex CLI](https://github.com/openai/codex), then run: ```bash cd hunterstick codex ``` Codex reads the root [`AGENTS.md`](https://developers.openai.com/codex/guides/agents-md) before working. The router in that file maps the user's objective to the relevant skill and playbook. #### Kimi — Kimi Code CLI Install [Kimi Code CLI](https://www.kimi.com/help/kimi-code/cli-getting-started), then run: ```bash cd hunterstick kimi ``` Use `/login` when prompted. Do **not** run `/init`: HunterStick already ships its canonical `AGENTS.md`, and Kimi automatically loads project instruction files, so it does not need to generate another one. `/login` only selects and authenticates the model/API provider; after it completes, name a HunterStick objective normally. #### Claude, GPT, Kimi, or DeepSeek — OpenCode Install [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai/docs/), then run: ```bash cd hunterstick opencode ``` Inside OpenCode: ```text /connect /models ``` Choose Anthropic for Claude, OpenAI for GPT, Moonshot AI for Kimi, or DeepSeek for DeepSeek, then select the model. OpenCode loads the root [`AGENTS.md`](https://opencode.ai/docs/rules/) and discovers the project [skills](https://opencode.ai/docs/skills/) under `.claude/skills/`. Provider-specific authentication is documented in the [OpenCode provider guide](https://opencode.ai/docs/providers/). > A chat-only web interface without persistent filesystem and shell access can discuss exported > HunterStick files, but it cannot safely operate or update the workspace. ### 3. Initialize the first target Tell the model what to create and provide the scope statement you received: ```text Initialize a new target acme. Scope is *.acme.com. ``` Initialization creates the target brain and stops without sending traffic. Then name one objective: ```text Run subdomain enumeration on acme. ``` Or start from an existing request or endpoint: ```text Analyse this Burp request for acme. Test IDOR on acme's /api/orders endpoint using the recorded accounts. ``` When returning later — even with another runtime or model — say: ```text Resume acme. ``` HunterStick reconstructs unfinished work, decisions, stale inputs, coverage, and the exact files needed for the next user-selected objective. ## Choose a capability You normally describe the objective; you do not need to remember repository paths or operate the Python tools yourself. The runtime uses `AGENTS.md` to route your request to the files below. The links are here so you can inspect, edit, or audit the fieldcraft the model will follow. ### Recon skills Every recon objective loads the shared [recon method](skills/shared/_recon-method.md) plus one focused skill. The shared file provides the adaptive tool loop; the focused file defines the required inputs, signals, traps, outputs, and exit criteria for that objective. The [skill library](skills/) is grouped by hunting intent so a hunter can browse it without knowing repository paths in advance. Categories are navigation only: ask for `http-probing`, and the runtime resolves its body under `skills/know-your-target/`. Invocation names stay stable if a skill moves between categories. Host-level skills accept either one exact host named by the hunter or the applicable target-brain host set. Naming `app.acme.com` does not require estate-wide enumeration first and never silently widens to its parent apex. Skills whose result only exists across several hosts—clustering and cross-host replay—remain explicitly set-based. | What you ask for | Focused skill | |---|---| | “Identify the organization's roots.” | [Organization and roots](skills/know-your-target/organization-and-roots.md) | | “Enumerate subdomains for acme.” | [Subdomain enumeration](skills/know-your-target/subdomain-enumeration.md) | | The complete repository map, including asset, infrastructure, synthesis, and handoff skills, is in [FILEMAP.md](FILEMAP.md). ### Vulnerability-hunting skills A vulnerability request enters through [vuln-hunt](skills/vulnerability-testing/vuln-hunt.md). The runtime then loads the shared [master hunting loop](playbooks/vulns/_master-vuln-hunting.md) plus exactly the class file you named. The [class index](playbooks/vulns/_index.md) maps broader requests such as “access control” or “business logic” to the applicable class files. Examples: ```text Test IDOR on acme's /api/orders endpoint using the recorded accounts. Check the search endpoint for SQL injection. Test the checkout flow for race conditions. Check access control across acme's recorded API surface. ``` Those requests load class files such as [IDOR/BOLA](playbooks/vulns/idor-bola.md), [SQL injection](playbooks/vulns/sql-injection.md), or [race conditions](playbooks/vulns/race-conditions.md). A class file is not a payload list: it teaches the model where the weakness hides, how to understand the function, how to design minimum proof, how to reject false positives, and how to decide whether the result is novel. ### Monitoring subdomains, hosts, and JavaScript Monitoring uses the [monitoring-and-diff skill](skills/monitoring/monitoring-and-diff.md) and [`tools/monitor.py`](tools/monitor.py). Enabling a recurring monitor is always an explicit user request; finishing recon does not schedule one automatically. The skill expects the target scope, the subdomain baseline produced by [subdomain enumeration](skills/know-your-target/subdomain-enumeration.md), and the live HTTP baseline produced by [HTTP probing](skills/know-your-target/http-probing.md). If one is missing, preflight names it and points to the skill that produces it. #### Passive subdomain monitoring Ask: ```text Monitor subdomains for acme every 12 hours. ``` The scheduled job re-enumerates in-scope names and records additions and removals. It sends no HTTP probes. The first run creates an immutable baseline and correctly reports no delta. #### Active host and JavaScript monitoring Ask: ```text Monitor subdomains, HTTP status and technology changes, and JavaScript changes for acme every 12 hours at 20 requests per second. ``` This enables the skill's active mode and monitors three independent dimensions: 1. **Subdomain names** — additions and removals. 2. **Status and technology on every in-scope name** — not only new hosts. A login gate appearing, an application replacing a placeholder, or a technology changing becomes a delta. 3. **JavaScript content on live `200` responses** — bundle filenames are normalized, while the raw body is hashed. A deployment that merely rotates `app.a1b2.js` to `app.c3d4.js` does not create noise, but a real content change produces `JS-CHANGED`. The model shows the interval, active dimensions, rate, JavaScript cap, and any exclusion it cannot translate mechanically before installing the requested job. Active monitoring requires a rate; program-required attribution travels with every probe. Discovered JavaScript URLs are checked against the target's domain allowlist and exclusions before they are fetched. Snapshots are never overwritten. Suspiciously small or incomplete runs are quarantined instead of being compared, preventing a failed source from producing thousands of false removals. A delta is new evidence—not a vulnerability and not permission to test it automatically. Use natural-language requests to operate the monitor: ```text Show the monitoring status for acme. Run the acme monitor once now. Show pending monitoring changes for acme. Disable monitoring for acme. ``` Underneath, the model uses: ```text tools/monitor.py status targets/acme tools/monitor.py run targets/acme tools/monitor.py pending targets/acme tools/monitor.py disable targets/acme ``` The pending delta remains available until a later user-directed session reviews it and decides whether to derive properties, re-prioritize the affected slice, or invoke a vulnerability skill. `brief.py --resume` performs a read-only monitor-status check and surfaces pending deltas, quarantined runs, and recent failures. It does not process or clear them. #### Notifications Configure any webhook channel — Discord, Slack, Teams, ntfy, Gotify, a Telegram bot — under `notify.channels` in `config.json` (a bare URL works; a custom payload template per channel is optional) and verify it with `tools/notify.py test`. Monitor deltas, quarantined runs, failed runs, new advisories from tech-watch, and the runbook digest ping it; per-run completion is opt-in. Delivery is fire-and-forget with a local spool, so a dead webhook never breaks a finished run. Payloads carry the target slug, event kind and one line — never commands or artifact contents — and `notify.strict: true` redacts even the target name. ### Other focused entry points | What you ask for | Files the runtime follows | |---|---| | “Analyse this Burp request.” | [Request analysis](skills/analysis/analyse-request.md) | | “Import this Burp or HAR capture.” | [Traffic-import workflow](playbooks/workflows/import-traffic.md) and [`import-http.py`](tools/import-http.py) | | “Recover the lazy JavaScript chunks.” | [Chunk-recovery workflow](playbooks/workflows/recover-js-chunks.md) and [`chunks.py`](tools/chunks.py) | | “Merge these saved jsluice/OpenAPI results into the brain.” | [`surface.py`](tools/surface.py) normalizes endpoints and parameters, safely reduces secret-shaped candidates without storing their values/context, and hands the resulting artifacts to property derivation without sending traffic | | “Run the dead-end-host flow.” | [Flow runner](skills/orchestration/run-flow.md) and the selected [situation flow](playbooks/flows/) | | “What does this Django/Next.js/WordPress stack change?” | [Technology analysis](skills/analysis/tech-analysis.md) and the selected [technology reference](playbooks/tech/) | | “Chain these several existing tasks.” | [Task composition](skills/orchestration/compose-task.md) | | “Show low-severity findings that may chain across these hosts.” | [`target-graph.py --chains`](tools/target-graph.py), [`kb.py chains`](tools/kb.py), and the [chain investigation template](targets/_template/investigations/chain.template.md) | | “Resume acme.” | [`brief.py --resume`](tools/brief.py), followed by the exact files it names | #### When no existing skill fits [Compose task](skills/orchestration/compose-task.md) is the last-resort escape hatch for a user-requested objective that no single skill, flow, or workflow covers. The model first checks that an existing capability does not already fit, then breaks the request into ordered steps, reuses existing skills where possible, and writes only the minimum novel glue for what remains. It states the plan, traffic, cost, and stop points before a pipeline that sends requests or fans out. ```text freeform user objective → existing skill steps + minimum novel glue → verify each step's inputs when that step starts → run every request through the normal execution and evidence harness → persist each output as the next step's input → update the target brain → report → STOP ``` The composed request remains **one objective authorized by the user**; it is not permission for the model to continue into unrelated work. If a component is missing a required input, the model names that input and its producer and stops there. The written plan, run record, evidence, and intermediate outputs remain in the brain so another session or model can resume the same pipeline instead of reconstructing it from chat. ## What is included - **35 skills** focused on recon, analysis, hunting, monitoring, importing, and task composition - **45 vulnerability classes** with variants, evidence expectations, and exit criteria - **10 situation flows** that bundle explicitly authorized multi-step responses to common dead ends - **14 analysis workflows** plus technology-specific context - **Small Python and shell programs** for preflight, execution records, surface normalization, coverage, context, graphs, monitoring, and target-brain maintenance Skills remain human-readable fieldcraft rather than generated command templates.
